title: Reading with family
hookLine: a household can share a reading, one page each
tomorrow: so where does anyone actually start a book this big?

cards: Nine at night, and the family group chat lights up: who's taking tonight's page? Yes, a whole household can share one long reading this way, a page each, passed from hand to hand like a relay baton.
Then the dad starts his page, and stumbles. He hasn't read Gurmukhi aloud in years. Some words come out wrong, and the room goes quiet.
Should he keep going, or hand the book to someone who reads it cleanly?

teach.h: ONE: LET THE CLEAREST READER READ.
teach.b: Two answers, and both come from love for the book. The first: let the strongest reader take the hard pages. The Granth is the Guru, and its sounds matter; a missed small mark can turn one word into another.
Reading it right is a kind of respect. And nobody's left out, because the rest of the family is listening, and the Japji praised listening first.

teach.h: TWO: EVERYONE READS, STUMBLES AND ALL.
teach.b: The second: everyone reads, stumbles and all. A shared reading is a small sangat, the household coming to the Guru together, and a page you read badly tonight is a page you'll read better next month.
Nobody learns Gurmukhi by only listening. Guru Nanak has a line in Asa di Var that both sides lean on.

In paraphrase: you could read cartloads of books, read every month and year you live; only one thing is counted, and the rest is the ego's chatter. The first side hears: it was never about who gets a turn.
The second hears: it was never about a polished performance. Something to tell someone tonight: some families settle it in between.

teach.h: A LEARNER, AND A READER BESIDE THEM.
teach.b: A learner reads, and a fluent reader sits beside them, quietly fixing a sound.
Either way the book is open, and the family is reading together.

how: Sikh households sometimes share a sehaj path, a slow reading of the whole Granth, with family members taking pages in turn; learners often read with a fluent reader beside them who helps with the sounds.

o: a family taking turns hosting the gurdwara's langar
parents reading Gurbani to small children at bedtime
sharing one reading of the Granth as a household

games.q: two views at one table — tap the pairs.
p: the clearest reader takes the hard pages
a fluent reader sits beside a learner

s: a family reading of the Granth has to be done by one person
a household can share one reading, a page each.

one protects the sounds; the other brings the whole household to the book.
Guru Nanak says the more you read, the more is counted
in Asa di Var he says, in paraphrase, only one thing is counted; the rest is the ego's chatter.

games.q: your uncle says only fluent readers should read in the family's sehaj path. you disagree. before you answer, what's his best case?
o: the Granth's sounds matter, and listening to a clear reading is itself taking part.
kids get bored, so it goes faster if the adults read everything.
stumbling is disrespectful, so learners should stay out of it.
games.why: that's his view at its strongest: small marks change words, and the Japji praises listening. your side's best case: a shared reading is how a household learns, together.

practice: If someone is near, read one line together: take turns word by word, or let one of you read while the other follows along. If no one is near, send one line you love to someone who might read it back to you.
Then sit with the line, and with them, for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Reading with family. One reading shared by a household, page by page, with room for the clear voice and the learning one. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sangat, the company of people who gather around the Guru's words; a family reading is a small one.

carryVoice: For the road: read together, stumbles included, with someone beside you to catch a sound. Good night.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467 (Asa di Var, salok Mahala 1: parh parh gaddee laddeeai… naanak lekhai ik gal, hor haumai jhakhnaa jhaakh), paraphrased
